Neurology · published research

Neuropathic pain (non-diabetic)

A 30-person uncontrolled pilot and a three-person amputation-stump case series reported pain relief after laser treatment. Most rodent nerve-injury models reported reduced hypersensitivity, but at least one rat study found no behavioral or biochemical effect.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 30-person uncontrolled pilot and a three-person amputation-stump case series reported pain relief after laser treatment. Most rodent nerve-injury models reported reduced hypersensitivity, but at least one rat study found no behavioral or biochemical effect.

Summary of the Evidence

After excluding one review devoted only to diabetic neuropathy, the mapped non-diabetic neuropathic-pain set contains 23 unique titles: two human reports and 21 preclinical publications. The animal records include three mouse studies, 17 rat studies and one report with species not stated. Two animal publications also include in-vitro or ex-vivo work, so laboratory results overlap with the animal publication count. These are not 23 independent human studies.

Human and clinical evidence

Iida et al. conducted an uncontrolled pilot in 30 people with neuropathic pain. Participants reported pain relief after laser treatment, but there was no sham or usual-care comparator (Iida et al. 2022). Ribas et al. described three people with refractory amputation-stump pain who received nine laser sessions; all reported lower pain and better daily activity during four months of follow-up (Ribas et al. 2012). These uncontrolled reports concern different pain syndromes and cannot estimate comparative benefit.

Animal evidence

Most rodent studies use chronic constriction, spared-nerve injury, spinal-cord injury or another experimental neuropathy. Many report reduced mechanical or thermal hypersensitivity after PBM, although effects differ by wavelength, timing and dose. One rat study found no behavioral or biochemical difference after infrared diode irradiation. Some papers combine PBM with swimming, chondroitinase or coenzyme Q10, which prevents attribution to light alone.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Two preclinical publications include cell or tissue assays alongside animal models, including measures of inflammatory signaling and pain-related pathways. No standalone human-tissue experiment was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols include red light around 660 nm, near-infrared light around 808–980 nm, and a polychromatic 600–1600-nm device in the human pilot. Routes include local irradiation of an injured nerve or amputation stump. The case series used 830 nm at nine sessions over three weeks. Animal schedules and exposures vary widely and cannot define a clinical dose.

Interpretation

The publications show that PBM can change pain behavior in several rodent nerve-injury models and describe pain relief in a few uncontrolled patients. They do not demonstrate comparative clinical efficacy. The small human samples and mixture of pain causes are the main limits on applying these results to neuropathic pain generally.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for pain relief in people because the human evidence is one uncontrolled pilot and one three-person case series. Low within rodent models for reducing evoked neuropathic hypersensitivity.
Publications and records23 unique titles after excluding one diabetic-neuropathy-only review

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The 23 mapped titles include 21 animal publications but only two uncontrolled human reports, with different causes of neuropathic pain. Two animal publications also include laboratory assays. Controlled trials should separate amputation-stump pain from other nerve injuries and measure pain, function, medication use and durability with a credible comparison group.
